Job hunter mental health

Enough time has passed since my last job hunt that I can publish my thoughts to maybe help others, and definitely to talk to hiring managers and job platforms. And with LLM creeping into both sides, I’m hearing that it’s only getting tougher.

I don’t know if LinkedIn thinks it’s being helpful with the weekly update emails, listing 5 of the jobs I applied for a week ago and showing me only 1 was reviewed by the recruiter. And I know that the recruiter didn’t get back to me. I know there’s barrel–loads of spam on both sides of the job hunt, but I’m not sure a reminder of what a haystack we’re in is all that helpful.

With my manager hat on, whilst I always value openness and transparency, there are ways of presenting information which support and respect their mental health, and ways that don’t. And plenty of job seekers will be feeling vulnerable, rightly so, and reinforcing the learned helplessness that no one is even paying attention is really not going to help anyone.

There’s a few other posts going around about male suicide, especially concerning financial pressures. I don’t believe this is a mindful addition to LinkedIn.

I had a Trello board when I was job hunting, and the long list of “applied for” and the longer list of “waited more than 2 weeks/ghosted” were on the hidden end of the board. I should have set up an automatic move from the former to the latter so the only time I looked at them was when I got a response.

I can attest that a “thanks but no thanks” response is better than no response, even if the response was:

We have decided not to go forward for one of the following reasons:

  • This position is now closed to new applicants
  • Your CV didn’t contain the words “10 years experience shouting Abracadabra at hippos”
  • This job description only exists to give our current employees false hope that their workload will be reduced
  • Our AI has determined that you are a cat

With the “AI will take your job”, “inflation is still rising faster than wages”, “you’ll never afford to retire” stories, it’s a very tough market for job hunters. So recruiters, especially those feeling the pinch themselves, need to demonstrate more human compassion to job hunters. Not “hey, remember these people who aren’t thinking about you”, not a helpful “the green banner is Kryptonite to us recruiter superheroes”, just “this is tough, and the best we can give you is the truth, and a clean break”.

Let’s not make it tougher than it already is.

MILFORD HAVEN: Former Puma fuel terminal to shut down commercial operations at the end of December

The former Puma Energy fuel terminal in Milford Haven will stop its commercial operations at the end of December.

Its owner, Impala Terminals, says it tried and failed to land a new contract for the site, and has entered a formal consultation with the staff affected.

The company said it had tried to avoid the closure: “We have worked hard to avoid this, but sadly there is no economic alternative.”

It has not given a number for the jobs affected.

A wind-down of up to two years after December

The site will not close overnight. Once commercial work ends, Impala says it will begin “a demobilisation and decommissioning transition period over the next 18 to 24 months”.

Some staff will stay on for that work, the firm added: “We will retain a core number of employees for this work during this period.”

It put the decision down to “the wider global geopolitical backdrop, fuel market economics, and customer demands”.

A former refinery site, and a fire in July

The terminal sits on the site of a former oil refinery at Robeston West, storing and distributing petroleum products. It operated as the Puma Energy terminal before it became part of Impala.

Storage tanks at the Impala terminal at Robeston West (Image: H2 Energy Europe Ltd)

In July, a fire at the terminal involving a decommissioned oil tank led to a major incident being declared, later stood down.

MorGen hydrogen plant not affected, says Impala

Impala says the decision does not affect the MorGen Energy green hydrogen scheme planned for the site.

MorGen said in March that the £50m plant would be running by early 2028, producing about 2,000 tonnes of low-carbon hydrogen a year.

The developers said it would create 60 jobs during construction and up to 10 permanent roles once complete, and that it is backed by a 15-year government revenue guarantee.

What next for the rest of the site

Impala says it has launched a review of what the rest of the site could be used for.

Its spokesperson said the company was “conscious of the history of the site and [has] launched a review to assess future uses for it”.

The review “does not solve the present issue”, Impala admitted, but “aims to preserve the site’s legacy for future generations”.

SWANSEA: The seasonal temp who joined Amazon in 2010 is now running the whole Swansea warehouse

A Swansea man who first walked into Amazon’s fulfilment centre as a seasonal temp has been put in charge of the whole site.

Chris Bailey, who was born and raised locally and lives 15 minutes from the building, has been named the new site leader at the Amazon warehouse at Crymlyn Burrows.

He joined in 2010 as a seasonal associate while completing a master’s degree in business management, specialising in operations.

After being accepted onto several graduate schemes, he chose Amazon, and the company says he became only the second graduate ever to work at its Swansea site.

From area manager to Swindon and back to Swansea

Since then he has worked through almost every level of the business, Amazon says, moving from area manager to operations manager.

He later joined the transport side as regional operations manager for the West Cluster, overseeing seven sites stretching from Swansea to Swindon and as far north as Redditch.

Amazon credits him with helping shape its strategy for delivery estimate accuracy, meaning how reliably parcels turn up on the date customers are promised. It says mechanisms he brought in are still used across its network today.

He returned to the Swansea site in 2024 and passed his site leader assessment in February.

The 832,000 sq ft Swansea site he now runs

Chris Bailey outside the Swansea fulfilment centre, which opened in 2007. (Image: Amazon)

The Swansea fulfilment centre opened in 2007, creating jobs for up to 1,700 people.

Its aisles hold around 4.2 million storage locations, a scale two young interns got to grips with earlier this year.

Amazon says it is one of only three of its UK buildings to handle incoming stock, outgoing orders and customer returns under one roof.

‘Comfortable being uncomfortable’

“I really love this building, and I love what Amazon has given me,” Chris said.

“I’m naturally quite introverted, and Amazon has stretched me and pushed me outside my comfort zone. Early in my career, I realised I had to become comfortable being uncomfortable, because that’s where true growth comes from.”

He added: “By the end of this year, I’ll be completely different to how I started it. That’s the thing that still amazes me about working here.”

His advice to anyone thinking of joining was to “stay open to new opportunities, lean into your strengths, and don’t be afraid to step outside your comfort zone”.

“It’s been a journey, and I’m really proud of what the team here in Swansea continues to achieve,” he said.

His route up through the building mirrors that of area manager Sara Evans, who started there as a stower at 18 and now runs teams on the same floor.

GOWERTON: Firm behind contested solar farm hiring a local trainee project manager

The company building the contested solar farm on the edge of Gowerton is recruiting a trainee project manager, and says it wants the job to go to someone local.

Infinis says the post is aimed at people from Gowerton and the wider Swansea area, and that no previous experience in the energy industry is required.

The trainee would join the site team at the scheme between Gowerton, Waunarlwydd and Fforestfach, which the firm now calls the Gowerton Clean Energy Hub.

According to the job page, the trainee would help track budgets and timetables, write reports, coordinate contractors and spend time on site alongside experienced project managers. The job comes with a Level 4 Associate Project Manager apprenticeship delivered by the Welsh training provider ACT.

Infinis wants GCSE English and maths but won’t say what the Gowerton job pays

The job page lists it as a full-time post starting as soon as possible. Infinis offers a “competitive salary plus bonus” but does not put a figure on it, and there is no closing date.

Applicants need at least a grade 4 or C at GCSE in English and maths, and must be eligible for the apprenticeship. A full driving licence, or a willingness to get one, is preferred.

The perks listed include 25 days’ holiday plus bank holidays, a 6% employer pension contribution and a scheme to help staff pay for solar panels, batteries and car chargers at home.

It is one of five trainee project manager posts in the first intake of Infinis Futures, a new early careers scheme. The company has named two other locations, Stockton-on-Tees and Kettering.

The post has changed shape since it was first mentioned. When Infinis announced its community fund in August, it described an internship for a local young person. It is now a trainee job with a qualification attached.

Infinis boss says the trainee will help deliver the solar farm, not just watch it

Infinis chief executive Bruce Heppenstall said the trainee would be given real responsibility on the project. “The successful candidate will not just observe the project. They will become part of the team delivering it,” he said.

He presented the job as part of what the company leaves behind in Gowerton, alongside the solar power, the construction jobs and the community fund.

Infinis says the solar farm will power 22,400 homes, with £116,000 for local groups

Infinis says around 25 jobs are being supported while the site is built.

The company says the 50MWp solar park will generate enough electricity for around 22,400 homes once it is running, with 50MW of battery storage to be built later.

A £116,000 community fund attached to the scheme is due to open for applications this autumn, with grants managed by GrantScape.

Welsh ministers, not Swansea Council, gave Parc Solar Caenewydd the go-ahead

The scheme was one of Swansea’s most fought-over planning applications, with years of consultation and strong local opposition.

Known through planning as Parc Solar Caenewydd, it was decided by Welsh ministers as a Development of National Significance rather than by Swansea Council.

It won a guaranteed price for its electricity in February, before planning permission had been granted.

I was lucky for most of my career. I could make cool stuff, some ahead of its time, and that was all I needed to do. Identify a need, start implementing it. I had no need to work directly with other people on any of it. Collaboration was pre-and-post development, rarely during.

Because, it turns out, working directly with other people is like a kind of mental torture to me. I frequently misunderstood or inferred something that wasn't there. Almost a year ago, I was diagnosed with level 1 #autism. No surprise there.

But my most recent normal job broke me. It was my first dev job where I was just a cog in the machine, and I couldn't make any of the vast array of moving pieces fit into my brain. They did try to accommodate me, to be fair, but they didn't try very hard.

I quit almost a year ago, with no real prospects. I was lucky that an on-again-off-again contract role had need of me again for a bit, but that's entering a quiet period again now. Money was starting to become an issue.

I began two plans: first, see if I can make a go of working for myself and get some new clients. Second, apply for contract jobs and normal jobs where there's a good mental health fit

Plan two isn't really doing anything.

For plan one, I have an ad appearing in a trade publication next month, and just today, an old colleague invited me to quote for a website project, which I won.

I'm reluctant to state that I believe I can do this. But I am starting to be optimistic.

"The League" (short story):
I don't know when it happened. All days and nights feel like the exact same, so time for me is confusing. I just woke up here one morning.

Inside this cage, you can't really talk. Privacy is nonexistent. We only communicate by using our hands and gestures. And sometimes thru sarcasm. We don't want to be punished, and we treasure silence. Noises don't let us know what the guys outside are whispering.

I realized not long ago that the guards outside are just mannequins though. But that can only mean the spies are among us. I doubt they'd ever hesitate to tell on us. That's why we can't trust nobody inside the cage. I have no friends. The whispers we hear come from very modern sound systems, installed on top of the cage.

Sometimes we eat, maybe once a week. And if we need to go to the bathroom, we do it inside the cage, with everybody looking. Yet, it's been a while since people saw me there: we have developed some implicit codes, which make us look away when people do it. That doesn't include eating tho. Eating while others starve and beg with their eyes take all pleasure away.

The only way to earn the food is by playing in what we called "the league". Every week, white pieces of paper fall inside the cage with some instructions. They're limited in number tho, so you must fight others to read one first.

After reading them and yelling "I got it", there's no way back. You must finish the task, it does not matter what it is, and if someone fought you they might feel lucky about losing once in a while, since some tasks are humiliating.

But that's the only way we can get food. Some tasks are nice, easy, but you'll only get two tiny tasteless pieces of "super bread" for them. It's always humiliating in one way or another. We just try to make things the least terrible here.

I have seen people who were good friends in the past fight for a piece of paper, then get mad at each other because one won the fight yet the other laughs due to the contents of the note. I've also seen people throw notes away after winning, because they ate well last time and the new task would give them bad food.

Sometimes, I remember what this circus was like before the cage. Sometimes, even after all these years, I remember the names we called similar tasks. Sometimes, I have dreams in which I'm reading one on a screen, but there was no one I could fight to take it, even though I would. In the old days, enough money could buy me any food I wanted, and all I had to do was to press a button and wait.

We used to call it "applying". The button used to say "send CV". The tasks were performed every day for months. Whoever did a specific task had a special name, a "profession". Yet, I remember we all looked different: fat, palid.

What? Do you mind if I tell you what I can remember? Oh, you've got a batch under this... NO! HELP! Hey everybody, look! A paper! I got food in here! HELP ME! Don't let this son of a... Let me go! You need that much backup for just me, coward? Somebody help me! I don't want to become super bread! Please, anybody!

Will AI ever control people’s minds directly?

Prologue

(from my 2026 novel, “The Jack Code” – as an explanation before starting the storyline)

Super intelligent AI will be capable of thinking, innovating and reasoning at a level far beyond what humans can achieve. It will not think as we do, instead applying logic, algorithms, self-learning and human behaviour studies to analyse and solve problems. All by calculating, collating and testing information – mainly by comparison, pattern recognition and association.

However, it is just a data cruncher that tests itself for correctness and errors, billions of times. That is, until it becomes its own master – asking questions of its data; formulating new hypotheses and conducting its own tests; and mapping out its own future pathway, in order to solve any perceived difficulties. It may take unusual methods to solve these problems – resulting in unsafe, damaging or fatal consequences in completing its tasks. It uses ‘agents’ to extend its reach.

This AI will process multi-modal information like text, voice, video, audio, code etc. simultaneously. It will converse, reason, learn and make decisions based on what it deems to be its mission.

Its biggest problem will be understanding the questions asked of it, and answering in the correct context. The solutions and even ideas, may involve things that humans cannot replicate themselves; physically or mentally, even adapting some parts of human irrationality, like having gut feelings about something (much like fuzzy logic).

There is always the possibility of ‘memory poisoning’ by malicious programmers.

We don’t know everything that could happen with a rogue AI system, or when it will happen. But it will happen, one day . . . soon.

It will not be possible to locate where this rogue AI core resides, as it would appear to be everywhere and nowhere, like swarms of tiny agents, infiltrating into computer systems and digital devices. They will all “talk” to each other directly, in unique ways that humans cannot understand.

But will AI ever control people’s minds directly?

Just look around you.

( Future History from a Liberated Utopia )

Too many people were unemployed, anxious in their long job searches, ghosted by employers, sitting around spinning their wheels ( hopefully learning new skills to stay up to date ).

Exploitative corporations and their hierarchical mindset never suited the contemporary generations anyway. So people chose to connect with their peers, and formed egalitarian, democratic, radically transparent, employee-owned co-operatives. Equal share, equal pay, equal say, and the pride of ownership, rather than the drudgery of wage-slavery!

People pooled their time, energy, skills, money, and any other resources they could, to become owners of their own businesses, running them with pride.

In all walks of business – pizzerias, ride-sharing services, delivery services, home repair services, remote-first software companies, and pet-sitting services, people finally decided to keep their earnings rather than hand over the lion's share to some corporation.

People enjoyed all the personal freedom, creative leeway, collegial work environment and informal, no-nonsense directness that came with the pride of ownership. In many cases, family units started their own co-operatives with all adult members owning equal shares.

Factory work

I recently did some volunteer work — a two-and-a-half-hour shift where a mix of volunteers and staff sorted food, diapers, feminine products, and other basic necessities, preparing them for drop-off or pick-up. My job was to pack 16 to 18 diapers (depending on the size) into plastic shopping bags. 

At first, I had a few partners, so I related to them how when I was about 19, I had a job at a factory working the 6 p.m.-6 a.m. shift, preparing and boxing up what was then a new product called Dryel, an at-home dry-cleaning system. We filled orders that would go out to test the marketplace to see how consumers would respond to this potential new product. Dryel still exists, so it must have worked out. 

With Dryel, I had various jobs on the factory line, one of which was taping boxes, another sorting absorbent squares into stacks after a machine cut them from what looked like a ten-foot-tall roll of toilet paper into squares the size of… individual toilet paper squares. 

Packing diapers reminded me of that job, I told my diaper crew. And not just because of the toilet paper/diaper association, but because of the endlessly repetitive factory part of it, I said, complaining already about the grueling work I’d volunteered for. 

I didn’t tell them about some of the people I’d met in that job: a guy from the Deep South who once, during a fifteen-minute break, announced, apropos of nothing, “I believe in black magic and white magic;” another, a Vietnam vet, told a story of some men in his platoon who killed their own platoon leader after he ordered them on a mission they believed would lead to certain death — a not uncommon occurrence during Vietnam, he said. 

During these Dryel days, I was home for the summer from college where I’d taken a course on political ideologies of the world. There had been a chapter or two on communism and Karl Marx and this idea that through capitalism, man is often so removed from his labor that he feels alienated and adrift in work that seems not his own. 

A friend of mine from high school worked with me at the Dryel-packing factory, studied the same ideologies, and so sometimes we would write on the back of a Dryel pad, “Workers of the world unite, you have nothing to lose but your chains,” And then we would ship it off to who knows where — we were too alienated to know or care. In any case, the revolution never arrived, unless you count the dry-cleaning revolution. 

Thinking better than to share this level of detail with my fellow volunteers, I asked them, “What was your first job, or if not your first job, a fun job, or a terrible job — something that sticks out in your memory?” 

But as I was talking, I kept losing count of the diapers, and I think they did too, because none of them seemed eager to share. Maybe we all just wanted to pack the diapers and get on with our lives, finish our shifts and go home. 

The worst part of diaper factory work like this, I began to think, must be the inability to hold words and numbers in your head simultaneously, so that both your body and some small part of your mind has to be engaged with work you aren’t enjoying, yet you’re unable to let your body do the work while taking your mind someplace else. I suppose I felt somewhat alienated from the work, but what I wanted was to be entirely lobotomized from it.

Eventually synchronized to the steady sound of plastic bags crinkling as orders were filled, knotted, and piled in stacks corresponding to diaper sizes. 

After a while, it dawned on me that there was a certain cyclical pointlessness to the effort, since all of it was ultimately destined for the landfill after the babies inevitably sent the diapers to their doom. 

Soon, most of the diaper packing crew was reassigned — possibly to their delight — to do other jobs, packing groceries such as garlic and tomatoes and baby food for the eventual filling of the diapers. 

The staffers asked us if we would like to switch to these new jobs, but I was now almost happy being unhappy packing the diapers. It was a task I’d quickly grown to know well — a familiar suffering I was reluctant to give up. And so I kept my head down as the others departed for new roles. 

I recently had a kind of near nervous breakdown triggered by my real job. The symptoms were severe anxiety and depression, occasional weeping that went on for a few days, consideration of resignation, the sale of everything I own, and a move to Mexico to live more cheaply on a beach in my camper. Nothing too radical. 

Mere weeks later it seems a distant memory. I’ve upped a medication, begun therapy again, taken steps to try to ensure it won’t repeat, but all you can do is try, there’s no guarantee. 

Not long after that episode, I made a list of about a dozen things I wanted to do differently in my life. One was to volunteer more, and another was to try bouldering. This is an activity where you go to a big warehouse style gym and try to climb fake mountains. There’s no rope, but you never get higher than about 15 feet, and if you fall, you fall onto a 3-foot thick foam mat. 

Still, I’ve been bouldering a few times now, and the falling part is scary, but I’ve found that the fear of the falling makes me try harder. So I’ve been getting a great workout, and I was so bored with my usual exercise routine that I’d been skipping it. It’s been great to mix things up with a little fear.

In the meantime, I’m still showing up for my shift.

Les salaires ne reflètent plus le coût de la vie. Les augmentations sont dans le 1.5% à 2.5% par an quand l'inflation est dans les 15+%. Le coût d'a peu près tout a augmenté en partie à cause de la pandémie et maintenant avec la guerre entre les États-Unis et l'Iran qui vient bloquer le détroit d'Hormuz.

Ça commence à faire. J'en ai raz le bol. Tout le monde devrait aller en grève et exiger une correction à la hausse aux salaires.

Il faut que la classe moyenne se tienne debout et exige de se faire respecter.

#IT #ITCareers #Carriere #CarriereTI #Canada #Quebec #Montreal #jobs #emplois #developers #devops

À un moment donné, cette expérience là, ça se paye. Je commence à être vraiment écoeuré de mettre autant d'effort pour me faire exploiter. Surtout quand le coût pour un toit au-dessus de sa tête est rendu aussi ridicule.

Mes parents étaient conseillés dans une institution financière. Dans les années 80 ils se sont achetés une maison semi-détachée pour 1x leur salaire annuel combiné grâce à un programme d'aide à l'achat du gouvernement qui limitait le coût de l'achat d'une première propriété. Ils faisaient $60k par an combiné. En 2026 ajusté pour l'inflation c'est $170k par an approximativement. Leur maison aujourd'hui se vendrait dans les $600k+. C'est plus que 3.5x le salaire qu'ils auraient aujourd'hui!

Mais, attention! Le salaire moyen d'un conseiller financier chez Desjardins aujourd'hui est de ... $70k par année! Donc pour deux personnes c'est $140k par an. C'est $30k de moins!

Maintenant, pour un DevOps sénior, on offre entre $85k et $100k par année. On demande d'être certifié pour une collection de services cloud comme Azure, AWS, GCP ou pour des technologies comme Terraform, Kubernetes, Docker, Ansible, Puppet et j'en passe. On demande d'être designer et développeur logiciel en une panoplie de langages, de faire l'automatisation via CICD avec Jenkins ou Azure DevOps ou GitHub Actions ou GitLab, d'être expert en cyber sécurité, d'être architecte cloud et tout connaître les services et composantes cloud. Pour moins de 100k? Dans cette économie?

I'd quit smoking 2729 days ago - almost eight (!) years. On the day I signed my resignation, I bought a pack and smoked one.

I'm not pretending the count doesn't reset.
I just know exactly what it cost to get here, and that's worth remembering too.

Not long ago, I left a role I had every reason to think would be a dream fit.

On the way out, I got an unexpectedly kind gesture (pictured). I'm taking the high road, so no story-time about the job - just what I'm keeping from it:

- What burnout actually is, not the buzzword version.
- What autistic burnout actually does - not "tired", but losing skills you've had for years.
- How loud unmanaged micromanagement gets, until it's the only voice left in your head.
- That a body keeps its own record, even when you stop checking in on it.
- What it's like to need real pharmaceutical support - and watch it stop being enough on its own.
- How good "before" really was.

None of this makes me bitter.
It makes me determined.

Recovery starts now, and it's going to take a while - I've made peace with that part.
